# Privacy vs experience (performance, usability) {background-color="#40666e"}
:::{.notes}
TABLE: 

- Real identity
- IP
- location
- Destination
- content / activity
:::


## Tor in one slide
:::{.incremental}
- Client picks 3 relays (Tor servers) from a public directory: **guard → middle → exit**
- Layered (onion) encryption: each hop peels off one layer
- Guard knows *who you are* (your IP) but not what you're doing
- Exit knows *what you're doing* but not who you are
- Middle glues them together without learning either side
- **No single relay can link identity ↔ activity**
:::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Draw three boxes in a line — Guard, Middle, Exit — with the client on the left and the destination on the right. Draw the layered encryption as nested envelopes: the client wraps the message three times, and each relay peels one layer. Label what each box can read after unwrapping its layer. This picture is worth spending two minutes on; every subsequent system is a simplification of it.
:::


## What Tor is buying you
:::{.incremental}
- **Unlinkability**: making it hard to connect your IP to your destinations
- Resistance to compromise of any single relay
- Resistance to local observers and partial network visibility
- Some friction against timing attacks: fixed-size chunks, layered encryption, multi-hop paths
- Protection even when the destination site itself is hostile
- This is a very strong privacy goal
- **No** protection against someone who can watch both your traffic into Tor and traffic leaving Tor
:::

::: {.notes}
Pause on the last bullet. The global passive adversary — someone who can watch both ends — can correlate timing even without breaking any encryption. This is the fundamental limit of mix-network designs. Also worth saying verbally: the "fixed-size chunks" point means Tor pads everything to 512-byte cells so packet sizes can't leak content. That's a real engineering cost.
:::

## What Tor costs you
:::{.incremental}
- 3 hops, often spread across continents → delay stacks up and is unpredictable
- Each hop decrypts and re-encrypts every small chunk of traffic
- Path is random, not performance-aware
- Bandwidth is donated by volunteers: scarce, congested
- Connections can get stuck waiting behind each other inside the chosen path
- Many sites *block* Tor exits outright
- Typical page load: **3-10× slower** than direct
:::

## The other extreme: VPNs
:::{.incremental}
- **One hop**: client → VPN provider → destination
- All your app traffic covered, near-zero performance penalty
- VPN provider sees: your IP **and** every destination you visit
- "We don't log" is a contractual promise, not a technical guarantee
- You replaced one observer (ISP) with a different observer (VPN)
- Several major VPNs have been caught logging despite "no-log" claims
- Marketed as privacy. Mostly sold for streaming and untrusted Wi-Fi.
:::

## The privacy ↔ performance dial
:::{.nonincremental}
|  | Direct | VPN | Tor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hops | 0 | 1 | 3 |
| Performance | best | ~no penalty | 3–10× slower |
| Identity hidden from destination | no | yes, VPN exit IP | yes, Tor exit IP |
| Activity hidden from the proxy | n/a | no, provider sees all | yes, split across hops |
| Privacy assumption | none | trust the VPN company | partial observers + malicious relays |

- Two extremes, nothing in between.
- *This lecture is about what's in between.*
:::

## The uncomfortable question
:::{.nonincremental}
Most people are not being hunted by an intelligence agency.

Most people **are** being profiled by their ISP, their DNS server, the advertising industry, and whoever owns the Wi-Fi they just joined.

Can we design a system that defeats *that* attacker, at a price (performance, experience) people will actually pay?
:::


## The core design pattern
:::{.incremental}
- **Split knowledge across parties that do not share logs or cooperate**
- Party A learns *who* you are, but not *what* you're doing
- Party B learns *what* you're doing, but not *who* you are
- Neither one alone can profile you
- This is the same pattern as Tor, but with **2 parties instead of 3+**, and *named* companies with contracts and reputations
- Trade-off: if A and B collude, you lose. 
:::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Draw two boxes labeled A (identity) and B (activity). Write "profile = A ∩ B" and put a wall between them labeled "must not cooperate." Then draw an arrow from an attacker pointing at the wall and write "subpoena / hack / acquisition." This diagram recurs for every system in the talk — ODoH, Private Relay, OHTTP, PGPP all instantiate it differently. Worth drawing it once here so students can map each case back to it.
:::

# Oblivious DNS {background-color="#40666e"}

<!-- ## Questions to consider
:::{.nonincremental}
- Why is DNS a privacy disaster, even with DoH/DoT encrypting the wire?
- How does ODoH separate "who is asking" from "what they're asking"?
- What does it cost, in delay and in trust assumptions?
::: -->

## Why DNS is a privacy problem
:::{.incremental}
- Every web connection starts with a DNS lookup
- DNS translates names like `calpoly.edu` into server addresses
- Plain DNS: sent in the clear, visible to your ISP and networks in between
- Encrypted DNS hides the lookup in transit, but the DNS server still sees:
  - Your IP address
  - Every hostname you look up
  - Timing, frequency, patterns
- Resolvers like 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 promise not to log, but you're trusting them
- A DNS server is a *single point of correlation*
:::

## Oblivious DoH (ODoH): the idea
:::{.incremental}
- Insert a **proxy** between the client and the DNS resolver
- Client encrypts the DNS query so only the DNS resolver can read it
- Client sends the encrypted query *through the proxy* to the DNS resolver
- Proxy sees: client IP + encrypted query
- DNS resolver sees: query contents + proxy IP (no client IP)
- Response is encrypted back to the client the same way
:::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Draw the flow left to right: Client → Proxy → Resolver. Then annotate: the arrow from client to proxy carries [encrypted query + client IP]. The arrow from proxy to resolver carries [encrypted query + proxy IP]. Label what each party can read. The key visual is that the encrypted blob passes through the proxy untouched — the proxy is a courier, not a reader. This sets up the HPKE slide.
:::

## ODoH: what each party sees
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Proxy sees**

- Client IP
- Which DNS resolver
- *Not* the query contents
- *Not* the response contents
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Resolver sees**

- Query contents
- Response contents
- Which proxy forwarded it
- *Not* the client IP
:::
::::

## ODoH: how the encryption works
:::{.incremental}
- **HPKE** (Hybrid Public Key Encryption, RFC 9180): the crypto primitive underneath ODoH
- Resolver publishes a long-term public key (distributed out-of-band, pinned in client config)
- Client generates an *ephemeral* key pair and performs a Diffie-Hellman exchange with the resolver's key
- Result: a one-time shared symmetric key known only to client and resolver
- DNS query is AES-GCM encrypted with that key → the proxy receives an opaque blob it cannot read
- Response is encrypted back to the client's ephemeral key; proxy cannot read that either
- **Why ephemeral keys matter**: each query uses a fresh key pair — queries are unlinkable even if the resolver's long-term private key is later exposed
:::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Sketch the HPKE exchange if the audience looks engaged. Resolver has a long-term key pair (PK_r, SK_r). Client generates a fresh ephemeral (PK_e, SK_e) for this query. DH(SK_e, PK_r) = shared secret → symmetric key K. Client encrypts query with K; sends [PK_e, ciphertext] to proxy. Resolver runs DH(SK_r, PK_e) = same K, decrypts. Key point: the proxy only ever sees PK_e and ciphertext — it has no way to compute K. The ephemeral key also means each query session is independent; compromising SK_r later doesn't help.
:::

## The trust assumption
:::{.incremental}
- **Proxy and DNS server must not share logs or cooperate**
- If they do, the system collapses to normal encrypted DNS
- In practice: run by *different organizations* with different incentives
  - e.g., Cloudflare DNS server + Apple or Fastly proxy
- Contractually and reputationally separated
- This is not math; it's institutional separation
- That's a real weakening vs. Tor. It's also why it's fast.
:::

## What ODoH does *not* do
:::{.incremental}
- Doesn't hide the web connection that follows; the ISP still sees you connect to the server's IP
- Doesn't hide every hostname leak in the browser/network stack
- Doesn't protect against a DNS server lying about answers
- It's one piece of a larger privacy story
:::

# Apple iCloud Private Relay {background-color="#40666e"}

<!-- ## Questions to consider
:::{.nonincremental}
- How do you generalize the ODoH pattern from DNS queries to *all* web traffic?
- What does Apple see, what does the third party see, and what does the website see?
- Why is this fast when Tor is slow: what's structurally different?
::: -->

## The pitch
:::{.nonincremental}
Apple iCloud Private Relay (launched 2021, iCloud+ subscribers):

- Works for Safari browsing, DNS, and unencrypted HTTP traffic
- Zero configuration, just a toggle
- "Apple can't see what you're browsing, your network can't see who you are"
- Claims *negligible* performance impact
:::

## The architecture
:::{.incremental}
- Two hops, run by *different organizations*
- **client → ingress → egress → target**
- **Ingress proxy** (first hop, Apple): sees your IP, does not see destination or your Apple ID (blind-signed tokens)
- **Egress proxy** (second hop, third party): sees destination, does not see your IP
- Client encrypts traffic to the second hop *through* the first hop
- Second hop assigns you a **new IP** from a pool, geographically near you
- Target website sees the second hop's IP, not yours
:::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Draw the four-party chain: Client → Ingress (Apple) → Egress (3rd party) → Destination. This sets up the nested tunnel slide. Label what's visible at each link: between client and ingress the outer connection (Apple sees your IP/ID); between ingress and egress the tunneled connection (Apple forwards but can't read it); between egress and destination a normal HTTPS connection. Stress that the client encrypts to the egress *before* sending to Apple — so Apple is carrying a box it can't open.
:::

## What each party sees
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="32%" .nonincremental}
**Apple (first hop) sees**

- Your IP
- That you're using Private Relay
- *Not* the destination
- *Not* the content
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="32%" .nonincremental}
**Third party (second hop) sees**

- The destination
- Content (if HTTP)
- *Not* your IP
- *Not* your identity
:::

::: {.column width="2%"}
:::

::: {.column width="32%" .nonincremental}
**Website sees**

- The second hop's IP
- Approximate region
- *Not* your real IP
:::
::::

## The nested tunnel: how Private Relay actually works
:::{.nonincremental}
**Setup**: QUIC (RFC 9000) runs over UDP with TLS built in. MASQUE (RFC 9298) extends HTTP/3 to proxy raw UDP so a second QUIC connection can be tunneled through the first.

Four independently encrypted layers:

| Layer | Endpoints | Who holds the TLS key |
|---|---|---|
| ① Outer QUIC | client → ingress (Apple) | Apple |
| ② CONNECT-UDP | ingress forwards UDP to egress | — (ingress is a pipe) |
| ③ Inner QUIC | client → egress (third party) | Egress only |
| ④ HTTP/3 CONNECT | egress → destination | Destination |

Apple holds key ①. Egress holds key ③. **Neither can decrypt the other's layer.**
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk through the table row by row. The key insight to land: the ingress (Apple) in row ② is just forwarding UDP packets whose TLS it cannot decrypt — it physically cannot read the inner connection because it doesn't hold key ③. If the audience is engaged, sketch the nesting on the board: draw a QUIC connection as an outer box, and inside it draw the CONNECT-UDP tunnel as a pipe, and inside that draw the inner QUIC connection as another box. Apple holds the lock on the outer box; the egress holds the lock on the inner box. Neither has both locks.
:::

## What Private Relay does NOT do
:::{.incremental}
- Not a VPN: doesn't cover *all* app traffic, only Safari + unencrypted HTTP + DNS
- Doesn't hide you from the website if you're logged in (cookies, accounts)
- Doesn't defeat browser fingerprinting: tracking based on browser/device details
- The new IP is *regional*; it doesn't look like you're in another country

:::

## What Private Relay does NOT do (cont'd)
:::{.incremental}
- **IP geolocation has always been unreliable** — and Private Relay now depends on accurate geolocation of cloud egress IPs to preserve your region
  - Sites that gate on country/region can misfire; services tuned to your local market can break
  - You're trusting that the egress pool is correctly mapped in every geolocation database, which it often isn't
- Doesn't help if Apple and the third party share logs or are both subpoenaed
- Not available in every country (China, Russia, Saudi Arabia, etc.; blocked or disallowed)
:::

## Private Relay vs. Tor: the scorecard
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Tor**

- 3 hops, volunteer-run
- Stronger defenses against timing attacks
- Doesn't fail just because two relays cooperate
- Designed for stronger attackers
- 3–10× slowdown
- Exits frequently blocked
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Private Relay**

- 2 hops, commercial
- Few timing-attack defenses
- Dies if Apple + second hop share logs
- Not designed for nation-state attackers
- Near-zero slowdown
- Looks like normal HTTPS, so it is hard to block
:::
::::

## The authentication problem
:::{.incremental}
- The ingress relay needs to know you're a paying iCloud+ subscriber or anyone could use it
- But if the ingress asks "who are you?", Apple learns which Apple ID is making which connections
- That breaks the whole point: Apple's ingress is supposed to see your IP, **not** your identity
- We need a credential that proves "paid subscriber" without saying *which* subscriber
- This is the **anonymous credential problem**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a good place to pause and let students feel the tension before giving the answer. Ask: "How would you solve this?" The naive answer — just show your Apple ID token — is exactly the wrong answer because the ingress relay could then log Apple ID + connection timing, which is a profile. The right answer involves cryptographically separating the act of authentication from the act of connecting.
:::

## Blind-signed tokens (used in many systems)
:::{.incremental}
- **Blinding**: device generates a random token, mathematically blinds it (multiplies by a random mask), sends the blinded value to Apple's token issuer
- Apple's issuer checks your Apple ID, sees you're a valid subscriber, signs the **blinded** token — it never sees the actual token value
- Device unblinds: strips the mask, leaving a valid Apple signature on the original token
- The signer (Apple's issuer) and the verifier (ingress relay) see different things and cannot link them
- When connecting: device presents the token; ingress verifies the signature is Apple's → "valid subscriber" ✓ — but has no idea which account it came from
- Tokens are single-use; the relay marks them spent to prevent reuse
:::

::: {.notes}
The physical analogy that works: carbon paper inside a sealed envelope. You put your token inside an envelope lined with carbon paper. Apple signs the outside of the envelope — the signature presses through onto the token inside. You open the envelope and hand just the token (with the imprint) to the relay. The relay sees a genuine Apple signature on the token, but Apple only ever saw and signed the outside of the envelope — they never knew what was inside.

The protocol Apple uses is Privacy Pass (RFC 9576 / RFC 9578), which uses a Verifiable Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (VOPRF) instead of classical RSA blind signatures — same property, more efficient. The "oblivious" in VOPRF is doing exactly the same job as "blind" in blind signatures: the issuer evaluates a function on your input without learning the input.

Key thing to stress: this is not just a policy promise. The math prevents Apple's token-issuing service from linking a specific token to the Apple account that requested it, even if they wanted to. The cryptographic separation is real.
:::

# Forward vs. reverse: OHTTP {background-color="#40666e"}

<!-- ## Questions to consider
:::{.nonincremental}
- Private Relay protects *all* traffic but needs client-side plumbing. What if the client can't opt in?
- What if a *service* wants to offer privacy to users who don't even know they need it?
- What changes when the operator of the proxy is chosen by the *destination* instead of the client?
::: -->

## Forward vs. reverse proxy privacy
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Forward proxy (Private Relay, Tor, VPN)**

- Client opts in, installs stack
- Covers *all* destinations
- Client picks the proxy
- Destination is unaware anything is happening
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .nonincremental}
**Reverse proxy (OHTTP)**

- *Service* opts in, deploys a gateway (front door)
- Covers only *that* service
- Destination picks the proxy
- Client can be a plain HTTPS client, unaware
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
BOARD: Draw two diagrams side by side. Left (forward): arrow originates at the client, goes through a proxy box, reaches various destination boxes — the client drives it. Right (reverse): the destination box has a gateway sitting in front of it; the client arrow hits the gateway first, no client-side config needed. The key flip: in forward proxying the *user* decides to use privacy; in reverse proxying the *service* decides to offer it. Ask: "Can you think of a case where the user can't opt in but still deserves privacy?" (Crash reporters, telemetry, safe-browsing — they phone home without user action.)
:::


## The OHTTP pitch
:::{.nonincremental}
Some services *want* to not know who their users are.

- Safe-browsing lookups: "is this URL malicious?" The service shouldn't know which user asked
- Password breach checks: "has this hash appeared?" Shouldn't be tied to your account
- Telemetry: "here's a crash report." Shouldn't be tied to your IP
- DNS (this is where ODoH came from)

In all of these: the content of the request is not sensitive; **the association between client and request is.**
:::

## OHTTP: the architecture
:::{.incremental}
- RFC 9458 (2023), generalization of ODoH
- Three parties: **client → relay → gateway → target**
- Client encrypts the HTTP request so only the gateway can read it
- Encrypted request sent *through the relay*
- Gateway decrypts, forwards to the actual target service, encrypts the response back
- Relay sees: client IP + encrypted request
- Gateway sees: plaintext request + relay IP (no client IP)
:::

## OHTTP: how encapsulation works
:::{.incremental}
- Same primitive: **HPKE** (RFC 9180) — identical to what ODoH uses underneath
- Gateway publishes a *Key Config*: algorithm suite identifiers (KEM, KDF, AEAD) + HPKE public key
- Client wraps the entire HTTP request into an *Encapsulated Request*
- Relay forwards the encapsulated blob to the gateway; the relay holds no key, sees only bytes
- Gateway decrypts with its private key, issues a plain HTTP request
- Response travels back as an *Encapsulated Response* — symmetrically encrypted to the same session key
- **ODoH and OHTTP converged on the same crypto layer**: HPKE was designed precisely for this "encrypt to an untrusted path" pattern
:::

::: {.notes}
KEM (Key Encapsulation Mechanism): how two parties establish a shared secret. The client generates an ephemeral key pair, does a Diffie-Hellman exchange with the gateway's public key, and both sides derive the same secret. The client sends its ephemeral public key so the gateway can do the same math.

KDF (Key Derivation Function): takes the raw KEM secret and derives proper symmetric key material. HKDF is standard. You can derive multiple keys from one secret — e.g., separate keys for request and response.

AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data): the symmetric cipher that does the actual encryption. "Authenticated" means a MAC tag is produced alongside the ciphertext so tampering is detected. "Associated data" is cleartext metadata that gets authenticated but not encrypted. AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are the common choices.

Pipeline: KEM establishes the secret → KDF derives clean key material → AEAD encrypts the payload. HPKE (RFC 9180) is a standard way to wire these three together — which is why ODoH and OHTTP both converged on it.
:::

## What OHTTP gives up
:::{.incremental}
- **Only works for services that deploy a gateway**; you can't browse arbitrary websites through it
- Each request is independent: no long-lived browser connection
- Higher per-request overhead than a warm connection
- No protection against the target *service* itself correlating based on content (logins, account IDs, etc.)
- If the request body contains identifying info, you've leaked it anyway
:::

# The broader landscape {background-color="#40666e"}

<!-- ## Questions to consider
:::{.nonincremental}
- How have other companies adapted the two-hop pattern?
- Where does the trust actually live in these systems?
- What's the next frontier, and where does this pattern start to break?
::: -->

## Google IP Protection (Chrome)
:::{.incremental}
- Announced for Chrome Incognito, rolling out 2024–2026
- Same two-hop idea: Google-run first hop → third-party second hop
- Targets specific high-risk domains from a "masked domain list" (mostly trackers)
- Not all traffic, just stuff where IP-based tracking actually matters
- Google's framing: "we want to shrink the fingerprinting surface, not rebuild Tor"
:::

## The pattern, generalized
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%" .incremental}
- Identify the parties that would profile you
- Decide which ones can see *identity*
- Decide which ones can see *activity*
- Ensure no single party sees both
- Use encryption to enforce the split
- Use commercial/legal separation to make cooperation expensive
:::

::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .incremental}
- Pay for it with:
  - Extra hops (delay)
  - Extra infrastructure (money)
  - A trust assumption that parties do not cooperate
- Don't pay for:
  - Strong defenses against timing/volume attacks
  - Nation-state attackers
  - Hiding your identity from the *destination*
:::
::::

## Where does this pattern break?
:::{.incremental}
- **Cooperation between parties**: subpoena, hack, or acquisition of both parties
- **Side channels**: timing, packet sizes, volume patterns can still leak clues
- **Fingerprinting above the network**: cookies, browser fingerprints, logins
- **Destination-side tracking**: the site itself is usually the biggest threat
- These mainly protect IP addresses. The browser/application layer is a separate problem.
:::

::: {.notes}
Dwell on the subpoena point. In the US, both parties can be served simultaneously under a gag order — the math guarantees nothing if the legal system compels cooperation. The acquisition point is subtle: if the same company buys both hops, the separation evaporates. Also worth asking verbally: "What does it mean that the destination itself is the biggest threat?" — the answer is that IP privacy only gets you so far; once you log in, create an account, or even just have a unique browser fingerprint, the destination can track you regardless of which IP you came from.
:::


## Scenario
:::{.nonincremental}
You use iCloud Private Relay all day. You're also logged into Google, Instagram, and your university account in the same browser.

**At the end of the day, how much did Private Relay actually help you? What would have had to be different for it to matter more?**

:::

::: {.notes}
Let them actually think quietly for 3 minutes — resist the urge to fill the silence.

During pair discussion, circulate and listen for:
- Students who say "almost nothing" (probably right, for this specific scenario)
- Students who say "it still helped against the ISP" (also right — worth surfacing)
- Anyone who notices the distinction between sites you logged into vs. sites you just browsed

In the share-out, the answer you want to land:

Private Relay protected them from two things: their ISP seeing which sites they visited, and unauthenticated sites linking their IP to their browsing. For everything they were logged into — Google, Instagram, the university — those services have a complete profile regardless of which IP the requests came from. The IP was never the identifying piece there; the account was.

The "what would have had to be different" question is the important one. Answers to draw out:
- Not logging in (browsing anonymously, no accounts)
- Using a different browser profile or a clean browser with no cookies
- The sites not using fingerprinting (screen size, fonts, etc.)

The takeaway to say out loud: *these systems operate at the network layer. The application layer — logins, cookies, fingerprints — is a separate problem, and it's usually the bigger one.*
:::

## The takeaway
:::{.incremental}
- Privacy is not binary
- The *right* architecture depends on who you are worried about
- For most users, most of the time: the **two-hop, non-collusion** model is the sweet spot
- It's cheap enough to ship to a billion phones
- It's a real improvement over the status quo (ISP + DNS + advertising profiling)
- Tor is still the right answer when the threat is real, just not the *default* answer
:::

# Pretty Good Phone Privacy  {background-color="#40666e"}

## What the carrier sees
:::{.incremental}
- Every cell tower your phone has ever attached to
- Approximate location, continuously, even when idle
- Every call, every SMS, every byte of data
- Tied to your **IMSI**, the permanent subscriber number inside the SIM
- Tied to your **billing identity** (name, address, payment method)
- Retained for years. Routinely subpoenaed. Sometimes sold.
:::

## Why IMSI is the problem
:::{.incremental}
- IMSI = the cellular network's primary key for everything you do
- The protocol *needs* a stable identity per subscriber to deliver calls/SMS
- Older networks could reveal this ID over the air, enabling **IMSI catchers** ("Stingrays")
- 5G encrypts it over the air, but the carrier still knows it
- Anyone with the IMSI (or access to the carrier's tables) can reconstruct your entire mobility pattern
:::

## PGPP: the idea
:::{.incremental}
- Schmitt & Raghavan, *Pretty Good Phone Privacy*, USENIX Security 2021
- Same 2-party pattern, applied to the cellular system:
  - Decouple **subscriber identity** from **network access**
- A new virtual carrier (MVNO) sits between the user and the underlying carrier
- Every PGPP subscriber gets the **same shared IMSI**
- Carrier can no longer tell two PGPP users apart
- Billing and login live at the virtual carrier, via anonymous tokens
:::

## PGPP: who knows what
:::{.nonincremental}
| Party | Identity | Location | Activity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carrier (pre-PGPP) | yes | yes | yes |
| Carrier (PGPP) | shared IMSI only | one user of many | encrypted |
| PGPP virtual carrier | yes (for billing) | no | no |

- Carrier sees activity but not *who*.
- Virtual carrier sees *who* but not activity.
- Neither alone can profile a user; same trust model as the other systems today.
:::

## What it took to build
:::{.incremental}
- Cellular protocols expect a *unique* IMSI per subscriber for finding phones, moving between towers, and billing
- PGPP turns "find this phone" into a group operation across all sharers of the IMSI
  - Costs some extra downlink traffic; measured to be modest
- Authentication is decoupled: tokens prove "paid customer", not "which customer"
- Deployable as a virtual carrier on top of existing carriers; no carrier changes
- Demonstrated on real 4G LTE infrastructure in the paper
:::


## PGPP: decoupling authentication from identity
:::{.incremental}
- The virtual carrier (PGPP) handles billing and knows who you are
- Network authentication uses **subscriber tokens**: a credential that proves "paid subscriber" without embedding your identity
- Token is issued by the virtual carrier; the underlying carrier validates it cryptographically but cannot trace it back to your account
- Analogous to a transit pass: the turnstile learns "valid fare paid," not "who paid it"
- Authentication keys in the SIM are managed by the virtual carrier layer, not the underlying carrier
- The underlying carrier never sees your name, address, or payment method — only a valid token
:::

## Why it matters
:::{.incremental}
- Cellular metadata, records about where and when your phone connects, is *worse* than IP metadata in almost every way:
  - Always-on, no off-switch, no "incognito mode"
  - "Tower dumps" hand law enforcement every IMSI in a 1 km radius
  - Sold by some carriers to data brokers
- PGPP shows the 2-party pattern applies beyond web protocols
- The cellular network was just another single point of correlation
- Whenever a protocol bottlenecks identity through one party, the same fix applies
:::
